Hi Giovanna, Greg here. You asked me what people ask a new engineer in the first ten minutes. I made a list on the plane, and it is always the same five. One: what is your background? Two: what exactly do you do here, on a normal day? Three: how long is your commute? Everybody asks that one, and nobody knows why. Four: what are you working on at the moment? And five, usually at the end, when the coffee arrives: what do you do at the weekend? That is it. Five questions, and the answer to each one is about four sentences. Nobody wants a lecture. I prepared my five answers before my first day here, and I still use them. Prepare yours. Ten minutes is not a long time when you know what is coming.

Hi Giovanna, it is Karen. One thing about your ten minutes, because I think about this a lot. Everybody loses a word. I lose words in my own language, in meetings, every week. The problem is not the word: the problem is the silence after it, when you stop and start again in Portuguese. So learn three small sentences and use them. The first one: sorry, could you say that again? The second one: I do not know the word in English, but it is the thing we use to move the earth. The third one, and this is my favorite: let me start again. People wait. Nobody is timing you and nobody cares about the word. They care that you keep going. In my first year here I said sorry, could you say that again about four hundred times, and here I am.

First she says her name, her age and what she does. Then she talks about her background and her degree. After that she describes a normal day, from the alarm to the end of the shift. Then she describes the site, and where everything is. Then she says what she can do and what she cannot do yet. Finally she talks about last weekend and about what she likes.
